questions.text: What goes into bread? Flour, water, yeast and salt. What about yours?
questions.answer: Bread can be made from those four ingredients, but many packaged loaves also contain fats, sugars, emulsifiers, preservatives or improvers. Pick up the bag: how many ingredients are in yours? Paste them into BOTIA and look at them one by one.

questions.text: How many ingredients does a slice of cheese need?
questions.answer: Cheese starts with milk, cultures, rennet and salt, but a processed cheese slice can be a very different formulation, with emulsifying salts, starches, fats or other ingredients. Check whether your pack says cheese — or whether the ingredient list tells a much longer story.

questions.text: Does cooking cream contain cream… or a whole formulation?
questions.answer: Some products are almost entirely cream. Others use thickeners, starches, stabilisers or fats to create the same texture. Open the fridge and compare the big word on the front with the small print on the back.

questions.text: Does chicken stock contain more chicken — or more things that taste like chicken?
questions.answer: Depending on the product, the flavour can be built with extracts, flavourings, yeast, fats, spices and flavour enhancers as well as chicken. Find 'chicken' on your pack and see where it appears in the list.

questions.text: How much strawberry does something need before you think 'strawberry yoghurt'?
questions.answer: The strawberry picture on the front can be enormous even when fruit is only a small part of the formulation. Check the percentage in yours, then see what else is used to create the flavour, colour and texture.

questions.text: It looks like juice. How many steps are there between the fruit and your glass?
questions.answer: It might be direct juice, juice from concentrate, nectar or a fruit drink with flavourings, sugar or sweeteners. Before looking at the fruit picture, read the product name and the ingredient list.

questions.text: What does a potato omelette need? Potato, egg, oil and salt. How many ingredients are in the supermarket one?
questions.answer: A ready-made omelette can need more ingredients to keep its texture, stability and shelf life. Pick yours up: comparing it with those four basic ingredients takes ten seconds.

questions.text: Does vanilla ice cream taste of vanilla because it actually contains vanilla?
questions.answer: It may contain vanilla, extract, natural flavouring, vanillin flavouring or a combination. Find the word 'vanilla' in the ingredients and see exactly what form it takes.

questions.text: How many ingredients does mayonnaise need? And how many are in yours?
questions.answer: A basic mayonnaise is oil, egg, acid and salt, but a commercial version may also contain sugar, starches, stabilisers or other ingredients. Next time you open the jar, turn it round first.

questions.text: Is that sliced 'roast chicken' really just chicken?
questions.answer: A chicken cold cut can contain water, salt, starches, sugars, proteins, flavourings and stabilisers as well as meat. Check the actual percentage of chicken, then count everything that comes after it.

questions.text: What makes a cheese-flavoured sauce taste like cheese?
questions.answer: It may be cheese, but flavourings, extracts, fats, starches and flavour enhancers can also build that cheese sensation. Find out how much cheese is actually in yours.

questions.text: Is wholemeal flour the first ingredient in the wholemeal bread you buy?
questions.answer: 'Wholemeal', 'multigrain', 'rustic' and a brown colour do not mean the same thing. Look at the first ingredient: that is where the answer starts.

questions.text: That product 'with honey'… how much honey is actually in it?
questions.answer: A spoonful of honey pictured on the front can represent a very small percentage of the recipe. Find the percentage on the label before letting the picture answer for the product.

questions.text: Is a chocolate milk drink just milk + cocoa + sugar?
questions.answer: It can be, but some also use thickeners, flavourings, stabilisers or different sugars to keep the taste and texture consistent. Check yours: how many ingredients come after the cocoa?

questions.text: What is inside a burger that looks like it is simply meat?
questions.answer: A 100% beef burger and a meat preparation can look almost identical from the outside and have very different labels. Turn the pack over: does it just say meat, or does a list begin?

questions.text: Coffee creamer. It sounds like cream. But is there any cream in it?
questions.answer: Some creamers contain milk or cream. Others create the creamy effect with fats, syrups, proteins, emulsifiers and flavourings. This is a good one: read yours before trying to guess what is inside.

questions.text: What do you picture when you read 'pâté'? Liver, meat, fat and spices?
questions.answer: Depending on the product, you may also find starches, proteins, sugars, flavourings, stabilisers or preservatives. Read one full label. Pâté is one of those foods where the ingredient list can beat your imagination.

questions.text: Is tomato sauce just tomato, oil and salt?
questions.answer: It can be very simple, or it can contain sugar, starches, flavourings and other ingredients. Compare two jars from the same shelf: they can look almost identical from the front and very different from the back.

questions.text: Is a cereal bar basically cereals?
questions.answer: It may need syrups, humectants, fats, chocolate, flavourings and binders to keep everything together and soft. Check what actually occupies the first few places in the ingredient list.

questions.text: Is a plant drink just water + oat, soya or almond?
questions.answer: Some are very short recipes. Others include oils, stabilisers, minerals, vitamins, flavourings or acidity regulators. Check how much of the ingredient pictured on the front is actually inside.

questions.text: Is strawberry jam just strawberries and sugar?
questions.answer: It may also contain pectins, acids or other ingredients used for texture and preservation. Compare one jam with another: same product name, surprisingly different recipes.

questions.text: Is that cooked ham all ham?
questions.answer: Look at the percentage of meat. The rest may include water, salt, sugars, starches, proteins, stabilisers and preservatives. The number you really want is not always on the front.

questions.text: Why does grated cheese stay so loose inside the bag?
questions.answer: Some grated cheeses contain anti-caking agents to stop the pieces sticking together. Check yours: does the ingredient list end with cheese, or does it keep going?

questions.text: Does guacamole mean mashed avocado?
questions.answer: It can be almost that simple, or it can be a recipe with water, onion, tomato, thickeners, acids and other ingredients. Find the avocado percentage. Two green tubs can have surprisingly little in common.

questions.text: What does hummus need? Chickpeas, tahini, lemon, garlic, oil and salt. What does yours need?
questions.answer: Commercial versions may add acidity regulators, preservatives or other ingredients depending on the recipe. Compare yours with the version you would make at home.

questions.text: Is green pesto basil, oil, cheese, pine nuts and garlic?
questions.answer: It can be, but many products replace some of those ingredients with other oils, nuts, starches or flavourings. Look for basil and pine nuts first. Then see what takes their place.

questions.text: Is vegetable soup simply blended vegetables?
questions.answer: It can also contain cream, starches, sugar, flavourings, extracts or flavour enhancers. Find the first vegetable and check what percentage it actually represents.

questions.text: What does a croissant need? Flour, butter, water, yeast, sugar and salt.
questions.answer: An industrial croissant may also contain other fats, emulsifiers, flavourings, preservatives and improvers. Find 'butter'. Sometimes the word you expect is much further down than you thought.

questions.text: 'Butter biscuits'. How much butter does it take before you picture a biscuit full of butter?
questions.answer: The recipe may combine butter with other fats or flavourings. Check the percentage: the front of the pack creates an image; the ingredient list gives you the proportion.

questions.text: Does a custard or crème caramel need twenty ingredients?
questions.answer: Milk, egg, sugar and flavouring can make a basic version, but industrial desserts may use starches, gelling agents, stabilisers and other ingredients. Count the ones in yours.

questions.text: 'High protein'. Fine. But what else is in it?
questions.answer: A protein pudding or dessert may combine added protein with sweeteners, thickeners, flavourings and stabilisers. The claim tells you one thing it contains; BOTIA looks at everything else.

questions.text: '0% fat'. So what keeps it creamy?
questions.answer: When an important part of a recipe is reduced, other ingredients can help rebuild texture and mouthfeel. Look at what comes after the milk or yoghurt.

questions.text: 'Sugar-free'. Does that mean it does not taste sweet?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. Intense sweeteners or polyols can create sweetness without sugar. Look for words you may never have associated with something sweet.

questions.text: Is a 'fruit' sweet mostly fruit?
questions.answer: The front can show strawberries, oranges or apples while the formulation relies on syrups, sugar, gelling agents, flavourings and colours. Find the fruit percentage before looking at the picture.

questions.text: What is in an energy drink besides caffeine?
questions.answer: It may contain sugars or sweeteners, acids, flavourings, vitamins and other ingredients. Do not look only at the milligrams of caffeine: look at the whole formulation.

questions.text: Is a sports drink just water with mineral salts?
questions.answer: Some come fairly close. Others include sugars, sweeteners, flavourings, colours and acidity regulators. Compare two bottles from the same shelf without looking at the brand first.

questions.text: 'Natural flavouring'. Natural, yes. But natural from what?
questions.answer: The term does not always identify the exact raw material you are imagining. When you read 'natural', ask one more question: 'natural from what, exactly?'

questions.text: E471. Four characters that can hide a surprisingly long story.
questions.answer: It is the code for mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids, used as emulsifiers, and the label does not always explain the raw material they came from. Find E471 in your kitchen: it turns up in places where it barely attracts attention.

questions.text: Why do some fruits look as if they have been polished?
questions.answer: Glazing agents can be used to protect the surface and improve appearance, including shellac. Next time an apple looks unusually glossy, you will know what question to ask.

questions.text: That perfect red in a sweet, yoghurt or dessert can have a name you were not expecting: E120.
questions.answer: Carmine, or cochineal, is an animal-derived colour made from insects. Look for E120 or 'carmine' on a red product in your kitchen.

questions.text: Gelatine tastes of nothing. That makes it easy to forget it comes from something.
questions.answer: It is obtained from animal collagen and can appear in sweets, desserts, dairy products and other foods. Which product in your home would you bet does not contain gelatine? Check it.

questions.text: Lecithin is in chocolate, spreads and many foods that mix fat and water. Where does yours come from?
questions.answer: It can come from sources such as soya, sunflower or egg, and labels may identify the source in different ways. Find 'lecithin' on the first chocolate bar you see.

questions.text: 'Modified starch' sounds like one thing, but it describes a technological function rather than a home recipe.
questions.answer: It is used to alter texture, stability or the way a food behaves. See how often it appears in sauces, desserts and prepared foods in your cupboard.

questions.text: Maltodextrin. It does not say 'sugar', yet it appears in both sweet and savoury foods.
questions.answer: It is a carbohydrate made from starch and used for several technological purposes. Look for the word in your kitchen. Once you find it once, you will start noticing it everywhere.

questions.text: 'Fruit juice concentrate'. It sounds like fruit. It can also contribute sweetness.
questions.answer: Concentrating juice removes much of the water and increases the concentration of its sugars. See how many products labelled 'no added sugar' use concentrates.

questions.text: How many different ways can a product taste sweet without the word 'sugar' appearing?
questions.answer: Sucralose, acesulfame K, aspartame, steviol glycosides, erythritol, maltitol… they belong to different categories and have very different names. Pick three 'sugar-free' products and see whether they use the same solution.

questions.text: 'No artificial preservatives'. Does that mean nothing is helping to preserve it?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. Formulation, processing, acidity, salt, sugar or particular ingredients can all contribute to shelf life without the front of the pack using the word 'preservative'. Read the list and ask yourself how it lasts so long.

questions.text: Why can gluten-free bread have a longer ingredient list than ordinary bread?
questions.answer: Remove gluten and you have to rebuild structure, elasticity and volume using other flours, starches, fibres, gums or emulsifiers. Compare the two breads from the back, not the front.

questions.text: A plant-based burger looks like a vegetable turned into a burger. Is it?
questions.answer: Some recipes are very simple. Others rebuild flavour, colour and texture using proteins, fats, starches, fibres, flavourings and other ingredients. Find out what the first ingredient really is.

questions.text: Want to know what a product really is? Start with the first three ingredients.
questions.answer: The front of the pack sells an idea; the ingredient list starts with the ingredients present in the greatest amounts under the applicable labelling rules. Pick up any pack now. Read only the first three. Then paste the full list into BOTIA.
